case_studies.title: The Role Specialization Model (RSM): Coordinating LLM-Based Tools in Agentic Software Development - An Exploratory Case Study
case_studies.abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into software development workflows has given rise to a paradigm known as Agentic Software Engineering (SE 3.0), in which autonomous agents manage full development life cycles under human supervision. This paper presents an exploratory case study in which three LLM-based tools, Antigravity (an agentic IDE with a Gemini 2.5 backend), Gemini CLI, and Qwen Code (local execution via Ollama), are coordinated according to a role-distribution framework proposed in this work as the Role Specialization Model (RSM). Three research questions guide the study
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of coordinating large language models in software development by building the Role Specialization Model, which resulted in successful coordination of three LLM-based tools. The model helps manage full development life cycles under human supervision. It improves autonomous agent management in software development.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage software development workflows, here is what to do: review your current integration of large language models, consider adopting the Role Specialization Model to improve coordination, and assess the potential benefits of autonomous agents in your development life cycles.
case_studies.relevance_tag: IT Infrastructure, Software Engineering, AI Deployment
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel approach to integrating LLM-based tools in software development, which is directly relevant to IT engineers. The proposed Role Specialization Model (RSM) is applicable in the real world and can be used to build or propose services to clients. The potential to improve software development workflows and integrate LLMs with development tools is significant.

case_studies.title: Rethinking Agent Security as a Networking Problem
case_studies.abstract: AI agents are rapidly becoming more capable and widely deployed, promising substantial gains in productivity and enabling new classes of applications. However, their growing autonomy also introduces significant privacy and security risks. Existing defenses are predominantly agent-centric, relying on the agent itself to detect threats and enforce privacy and security policies. This approach is fundamentally limited because it entrusts policy enforcement to AI agents whose LLM-driven behavior is inherently nondeterministic and vulnerable to manipulation through attacks such as prompt injection.
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of securing AI agents by treating it as a networking issue, the authors built a new approach to agent security, and the result is a more robust defense against privacy and security risks. The study aims to reduce the risks associated with autonomous AI agents. It proposes a new way to think about agent security.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses AI agents, here is what to do: review your current security policies, assess the risks of prompt injection attacks, and consider adopting a network-centric approach to agent security to reduce vulnerabilities.
case_studies.score_reasoning: This paper proposes a new framework for agent security that rethinks the problem as a networking issue. The authors argue that existing defenses are inadequate due to the nondeterministic behavior of LLM-driven agents. This is highly relevant to IT professionals who manage and deploy AI-powered agents. They could use this information to flag a risk or propose a service to a client within 3 months. The proposed approach may lead to more secure and reliable AI deployments, which could have a significant impact on the IT industry.

case_studies.title: Beyond Trial-and-Error: Agentic Optimization for Image-to-Video Adherence
case_studies.abstract: Modern black-box Image-to-Video (I2V) models offer powerful capabilities in automated content creation, yet their lack of fine-grained control and reliability presents significant challenges in professional workflows. Their inherent stochasticity causes minor variations in textual prompts or hyperparameters to yield drastically different outputs often necessitating inefficient, brute-force trial-and-error processes. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of unreliable Image-to-Video models by introducing a new framework for goal-directed optimization. The team built the Agentic Self-Improvement framework to improve the control and reliability of video synthesis. The result is a more efficient and directed approach to video creation, reducing the need for trial-and-error processes.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving the capabilities of Image-to-Video models for content creation, rather than managing cloud infrastructure or related systems.
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty in the concept of Agentic Self-Improvement, some direct relevance especially in LLM APIs and agentic systems, but low value in direct applicability within 90 days as well as little potential for monetisation.

case_studies.title: Towards Automated Domain Model Extraction from Source Code using Heuristics and Open-Source LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong capabilities for code understanding, making them promising for reverse engineering domain models from source code. However, state-ofthe- art proprietary LLMs cannot be used in many industrial contexts due to privacy and confidentiality constraints, while compact open-source LLMs that can run locally are limited by their context window and cannot process large code bases directly. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of extracting domain models from source code, by building an automated approach using open-source large language models, resulting in a method that can extract domain models from source code locally. The approach combines structural heuristics with locally deployable models. This allows for private and confidential code analysis.

case_studies.title: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
case_studies.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for human-AI interaction typically relies on a single large language model to simulate user behavior. We show that this approach systematically fails to generalize, and trace the failure to simulator collapse: because the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, an LLM policy trained against it overfits to narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's dominant mode, and such a policy transfers poorly to unseen simulators and real users. We formalize this collapse theoretically and propose two complementary solutions, one at inference time and one at training time. T
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of simulator collapse in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where a single large language model fails to generalize user behavior. The authors built a theoretical framework to understand this issue and proposed two solutions to address it. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on machine learning and AI simulation. If your organization is involved in AI or machine learning development, this research may be of interest, but it does not affect cloud infrastructure management. No specific action is required for IT infrastructure managers.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty is moderate due to the exploration of simulator collapse. IT Relevance is high because it involves LLMs and RL policies. Value is low as the focus is on theoretical solutions and simulator design rather than real-world implementation or deployment.

case_studies.title: SAG: SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation with Query-Time Dynamic Hyperedges
case_studies.abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has proven effective at giving LLMs access to external knowledge, mainstream dense-retrieval implementations remain inherently limited in handling structured constraints and multi-hop reasoning. Graph-based methods address this by constructing knowledge graphs offline, but they often fragment semantics, incur high maintenance, and complicate incremental updates. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limitations in retrieval-augmented generation by building a new architecture called SAG, which organizes documents into an event-entity index. The result is a more effective and efficient way of handling structured constraints and multi-hop reasoning. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: No One to Blame: A Framework of Constitutive AI Unaccountability
case_studies.abstract: The increasing deployment of autonomous, agentic AI systems challenges traditional accountability mechanisms. Existing research predominantly frames AI accountability gaps as barriers that can be overcome through better standards, transparency, and institutional reform. We argue that this framing is insufficient: certain configurations of actors, systems, and institutions render AI accountability conceptually unachievable regardless of effort. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of accountability in autonomous AI systems, introducing the concept of constitutive AI unaccountability, and builds a framework to capture configurations where accountability is unachievable. The result is a deeper understanding of AI accountability gaps that cannot be overcome by traditional means. The study's findings are more relevant to AI ethics and governance than to IT infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the conceptual and institutional aspects of AI accountability rather than technical implementation or management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper discusses theoretical AI accountability framework but with little IT relevance. IT engineer may find some novelty in concept of constitutive unaccountability, but it's unlikely to affect their direct work or deployment practices.

case_studies.title: Is Per-Agent Policy Composition Safe? Rethinking Successor-Feature Transfer in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
case_studies.abstract: Many reinforcement learning systems, from fleet management to traffic signal control, must serve an objective that changes dynamically after deployment, and retraining a policy for each new objective is prohibitively expensive. The authors built a system to test the safety of per-agent policy composition in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. The result highlights potential risks in current approaches, but the research is not directly relevant to general IT infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: TRACES: A Benchmark for Epistemic Reliability in Scientific Reasoning by LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Large language models are being proposed as agents in scientific workflows, in domains where no downstream verifier exists. Such deployment assumes the model can distinguish reliable scientific literature from unreliable literature, a capability that has not yet been directly measured. Existing benchmarks evaluate factuality on questions with known answers; the failure mode we target here is different. We introduce a probe corpus of 42 retracted, fraudulent, and pseudoscientific papers, paired with a methodology for eliciting and scoring single-shot model engagement with each paper's framing.
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of measuring the reliability of large language models in scientific reasoning by building a benchmark called TRACES, which tests their ability to distinguish between reliable and unreliable scientific literature. The result is a methodology for evaluating the epistemic reliability of large language models. This does not directly affect cloud infrastructure management work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty is moderate due to an unusual benchmark, but IT relevance is low because there's no clear connection to IT infrastructure or practices. Value in 90 days is low because there's no clear action or automation that IT engineers can apply.

Prior literature has argued that cooperation problems such as the Prisoner's Dilemma are resolvable in settings where agents know they follow very similar decision making patterns, as for example in monocultural AI ecosystems. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of cooperation between Large Language Model (LLM) agents by introducing a framework that uses similarity signals to induce cooperation, resulting in mutually beneficial outcomes. The researchers built a framework to evaluate LLM decision making with graded similarity signals. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
